## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ajāta Sutta* ("Unborn", Iti 43; PTS It 37) is a concise doctrinal discourse situated in the *Itivuttaka* of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. Its teaching centers on the proclamation that there exists an unborn (*ajāta*), unbecome (*abhūta*), unmade (*akata*), and unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) reality; because this unfabricated dimension exists, an escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned is possible [SuttaCentral; Schmidt-Leukel 2006; Notz 2001].

This passage serves as one of the most prominent canonical statements on the nature of *nibbāna* and has played a significant role in Buddhist exegesis and philosophical debate [Schmidt-Leukel 2006; Notz 2001]. In late classical Indian scholasticism, the formula was central to Abhidharma controversies regarding the ontological status of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [Dhammajoti 2007; Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 2306 p]. Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika masters cited this sūtra alongside related texts to argue that *nirvāṇa* is a truly existent entity (*padārtha*), whereas opponents such as the Sautrāntikas argued that the phrase "there is the unborn" denotes merely the nominal discontinuation or non-arising of conditioned factors (*janmāpravṛtti*) rather than an independent real entity [Dhammajoti 2007; Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 2306 p]. In the Theravāda tradition, Buddhaghosa cited the passage to demonstrate that *nibbāna* is the sufficient condition of spiritual release [Schmidt-Leukel 2006].

Identical or closely matching formulations appear elsewhere in Buddhist literature, most notably in the *Udāna* (Ud 8.3) and in Sanskrit parallels such as the *Udānavarga* (26.21) [Schmidt-Leukel 2006; Svensk Missionstidskrift 2002; Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 2306 p]. DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse, showing an exact match with the *Tatiyanibbānapaṭisaṁyutta Sutta* (Ud 8.3, §2.1–2.3) and substantial shared material with the *Paññattihāravibhaṅga* (Ne 14) [DharmaNexus]. Formulaic prose passages are also shared with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Dhātu Saṁyutta* (SN 14), and other *Itivuttaka* texts [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus detects textual reuse in the Tibetan translation of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (D4061) [DharmaNexus].
